title: Behar: the land rests (Leviticus 25:1–7)
hook: every seventh year the land lies fallow and its produce is open to all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emor ended with one law for the stranger and the home-born. Your line was one law for all. Today, a new portion, and a Sabbath for the soil.

A farmer is told: for one whole year out of every seven, don't sow. Don't prune the vines. Don't harvest the way you normally would. Whatever grows by itself is food for everyone, including the hired workers, the settler, and even the wild animals. On paper, it sounds like a recipe for hunger. In modern Israel, farmers and rabbis still wrestle over how to keep it. And the Torah opens this portion with a strange address: it says this was spoken at Mount Sinai.
screen: `ONE YEAR IN SEVEN: DON'T PLANT.` → `ANYONE MAY TAKE.` → `SPOKEN AT MOUNT SINAI.`

segments.voice: When you come into the land, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD." Six years you sow and harvest. The seventh is the year tradition calls shmita, a release, and the land lies fallow. What grows on its own is for everyone: you, your servants, your hired worker, the settler living with you, your cattle, and the wild animals in your land. For a year, the owner's fence means less. The rich farmer and the poor stranger eat from the same field. Then, why Sinai? Rashi asks what the sabbatical year has to do with Mount Sinai. Weren't all the commandments given there? His answer: just as shmita was given at Sinai with its general rules and its fine details, so were all the others. And look back at the week. As yourself closed Kedoshim. Emor said it twice, set the appointed times, counted fifty days, fed the poor at the feast, and gave one law for all. Now Behar, on the mountain, lets the ground rest. Shmita is still observed in Israel, in different ways in different communities. Elsewhere, people borrow its rhythm: a sabbatical, a fallow season, a year of letting something lie.
screen: `SHMITA: THE SEVENTH-YEAR RELEASE.` · `THE FIELD IS OPEN TO ALL.` · `WHY SINAI? RASHI ASKS.` · `A WEEK FROM KEDOSHIM TO BEHAR.` · then, large: `THE LAND RESTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that's been worked every single day without a break: your body, a relationship you keep managing, a project, a habit of always optimizing. What would it mean to let it rest for a day, a week, a season? Not to abandon it, but to leave the soil alone so it can recover.
Shmita. The release: the seventh year, when the land of Israel rests and what grows is open to everyone, people and animals alike.
Your line: the land rests too. Rest is part of the work, not a break from it. Another week behind you, day four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In Israel the shmita year is observed by some farmers and consumers, through fallowing, special arrangements for produce, or a contested legal sale of land; outside Israel, Jews study its laws and some communities mark the year with learning and giving.

what a scholar hears: Leviticus 25:1–7 sets the land's sabbath; the noun shmita (release) comes from Deuteronomy 15, and Exodus 23:11 uses its verb; Rashi's 'what has shmita to do with Sinai?' comes from the Sifra.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 25:2 'then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD.' quoted from memory; confirm.
The noun 'shmita' appears in Deut 15:1–2 (release of debts); Exodus 23:11 uses the verb (tishmetenah). Lev 25 itself speaks of the land's sabbath. Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Modern observance: heter mechira (sale permit), otzar beit din, and other arrangements are debated; howItsDone says 'contested legal sale'. Confirm tone.
